title: Iceberg tables
summary: Every Timelake table is a plain Apache Iceberg table of Parquet files, so DuckDB, Spark, Trino, Snowflake and Athena read it with no Timelake software. Timelake adds its time-series conventions only through Iceberg's extension points (table properties, snapshot summaries, sidecar files), which other engines ignore.

title: Commits
summary: Every append, compaction and upgrade is one atomic Iceberg commit, made by Timelake's own commit layer on iceberg-rust's public types. Concurrent writers are safe without a catalog service: a conflicting commit is rebased and retried. Commits take two steps: everything uploaded in parallel, then one conditional write.

title: Object-store catalog
summary: Tables are committed through the object store alone: `vN.metadata.json` written with put-if-absent, plus a version hint, in the layout of Iceberg's Hadoop catalog. Plain DuckDB and Spark read the tables with no catalog service, and concurrent writers need nothing but the bucket.

title: Time-series table contract
summary: Users define their own schema; a table becomes a Timelake table by declaring a time column and, optionally, a series key, dedup and a chunk interval, stored as `timelake.*` table properties. The contract drives the layout, dedup, retention and rollups. Creating tables with a contract is built; adopting existing Iceberg tables is planned.

title: File layout and encodings
summary: How a Timelake table's data sits in Parquet: time partitions from the contract, files sorted by (series…, time), 1M-row row groups with page indexes, delta-encoded times, dictionary-encoded values (floats falling back to byte-stream-split) and ZSTD. Parquet stays the format; Vortex was measured and kept for places Timelake owns the read path.

title: Last-value index
summary: The latest row of every series, kept in a small Parquet file per snapshot, so "the current state of every device" is answered in a few requests instead of a scan. Latest-row queries are rewritten onto it automatically. It works at hundreds of thousands of series; making its cost per commit independent of the series count is open.

title: One-request table state and version checks
summary: Each commit also writes a head object with the table's metadata, live files, the last-value index and Parquet footers, so a cold query plans after one GET instead of six or seven dependent requests. Readers validate it with a listing or a check for the next version, and may reuse a checked version for `version-check-interval`.

title: Table format versions and upgrades
summary: Tables record a table format version, a semantic version of its own separate from Timelake's, so a Timelake refuses tables it can't read or write correctly. `timelake upgrade` brings tables to the current format without data loss, as ordinary commits that `timelake rollback` can undo.

title: Settings
summary: Every engine feature has a setting that turns it on or off or picks its behaviour, at the table, session or call level, declared once in a registry that drives validation, `SHOW`, the CLI and the docs.

title: Supplemental timestamps
summary: Declare the other times a sample carries (server, gateway, sent, corrected) in the contract, choose which time decides the latest copy of a row (`latest-by`), record per commit the ranges and delays of each time, and query a table as of an insertion time. Proposed, waiting for review.

title: Appends
summary: An append takes Arrow batches, aligns them to the table's schema, sorts them by (partition, series…, time), keeps the last of equal keys, writes Parquet in the table's layout and commits it, then runs inline maintenance. Writers batch rows and commit every few seconds or megabytes; batch IDs make retries safe.

title: Late data and dedup on read
summary: Late data is normal: it lands in its time partition and each commit records the ranges it touched. Copies of a row are removed by compaction and on read (the latest write wins by insertion time, then commit order); cold partitions compact sooner so dedup on read only touches recent data.

title: Writes from WebAssembly
summary: Append to and maintain tables from Cloudflare Workers and other JavaScript runtimes: the shared write path (rows, file writer, Iceberg manifests, commits, maintenance) in `timelake-format`, driven by `@timelake/client` through a store. Built and measured in workerd.

title: Hot tier and seconds-fresh reads
summary: Data visible to the Timelake reader within about a second of being written, before it is committed to the lake. Freshness comes in three modes: lake only (built), an object-store WAL (about 1 s, no extra infrastructure), and a managed hot store (sub-second); the reader merges the hot tier after each commit's WAL high-water mark.

title: Backfill
summary: Load months or years of history into a live table with one command: written in the final layout, staged on an Iceberg branch, validated, published atomically, resumable, with rollups refreshed afterwards. Existing rows win on conflict by default.

title: Import and migration
summary: `import` infers a table contract from a source, creates the table and loads it through the backfill engine: CSV, Parquet and Iceberg first, then TimescaleDB and Postgres with a `--sync` cutover, then the long tail through DuckDB. CSV and Parquet import with schema inference is built; the rest is planned.

title: Deletes
summary: Deletes never mutate data: a logical delete adds deletion vectors and an audit record and can be undone; retention drops whole partitions (built); a purge is the explicit, audited, irreversible exception.

title: GDPR erasure
summary: Erasure of a data subject: an immediate logical delete across every table, then a batched physical purge (daily by default, `--now` on demand, alerts past 7 days) that reaches every copy, verified and certified without logging personal data.

title: Compaction
summary: Compaction merges small files into large ones sorted by (series…, time), removing copies of rows (the latest write wins), so tables stay fast without Glue or Spark jobs. It is a streaming k-way merge with memory of one batch per input, shared by the engine and the WebAssembly writer. Inline compaction is size-tiered; cold partitions are rewritten into one file.

title: Maintenance runs, retention and expiry
summary: The jobs Timelake replaces Glue with (compaction, rollup refresh, retention, snapshot expiry and file cleanup) run inline after appends when thresholds are met, or as one stateless `timelake maintain` command. Nothing outside Timelake has to be scheduled. Orphan-file cleanup and sharded runs are open.

title: Timelake reader
summary: The Timelake reader (CLI, Rust, Python, and a WebAssembly reader for JavaScript) runs SQL on DataFusion over Timelake tables, and uses what a generic engine doesn't know: dedup on read, the last-value index, rollup routing, series-aware scans, time-series functions, and I/O tuned for object storage. Plain DuckDB still reads the same tables ([spec 1](0001-iceberg-tables.md)).

title: Block cache
summary: A caching layer under every read: immutable objects (data files, manifests, index files) in 1 MiB blocks, in memory and optionally on local disk shared by processes, with a read's missing blocks fetched together in GETs of at most 1 MiB. Repeat queries on S3 run at local speed.

title: Filter pushdown
summary: Late materialization: the reader applies filters while decoding Parquet and decodes the other columns only for rows that pass. It helps on local disk and costs a round trip per row group on object storage, so the default turns it on for local files only.

title: Pruning with long IN lists
summary: `column IN (…)` filters of more than 20 values skip row groups and pages whose range holds none of the values, which DataFusion's pruning leaves alone. On object storage the same pruning uses a join's runtime filter, so a dashboard over a list of devices reads only their pages.

title: Newest-first scans
summary: `ORDER BY time DESC LIMIT k`, and the k newest buckets of a `GROUP BY time_bucket(…)`, read time partitions newest first and stop once older partitions can't hold a row of the answer. "The latest readings before a time" and "the last few buckets" stop scanning the whole table.

title: Scans in series order
summary: Queries that work through each series in time order (signal aggregates, and windows partitioned by the series key and ordered by time) read files so that each series arrives whole and in order: files in time order, each scan partition a contiguous stretch of time, and only the files that overlap merged in series order. No repartitioning or sorting.

title: Materialized rollups
summary: A rollup is a Timelake table of aggregates per time bucket, defined in SQL, refreshed incrementally from the raw table's changed buckets, and used automatically by the reader with exact answers. Coarser queries and fewer keys are answered by re-aggregating a rollup, and wider rollups are computed from narrower ones.

title: Function library
summary: Time-series SQL functions with descriptive names and pandas aliases: bucketing, gap filling, selection, statistics, quantiles, changes, time-weighted aggregates, downsampling, rolling windows. Functions with a design of their own have their own spec; the rest are listed here with their issues. Built so far: `time_bucket`, `time_buckets`, the fills, the signal aggregates, the gap aggregates, `m4`, and `first`, `last` and `value_at`.

title: Time buckets and gap filling
summary: `time_bucket` groups readings into fixed-width buckets; the table function `time_buckets(width, start, end [, origin])` lists every bucket of a range, empty ones included, to join readings against; and the window functions `forward_fill`, `backward_fill` and `interpolate` fill the empty ones. Together they give one row per bucket for charts and reports.

title: Signal aggregates
summary: `time_weighted_mean`, `integral`, `counter_diff` and `counter_rate` over irregular readings, exact, as fast as `avg`. They share one mergeable state (runs of readings), which rollups store and several aggregates of one column compute once; a condition counts as 1 while true, for time in a state and uptime. `gap_count` and `gap_seconds`, how often and how long readings stopped, are run aggregates of the same kind.

title: Downsampling with m4
summary: `m4(time, value)` returns a group's first, smallest, largest and last points, a mergeable state that rollups store and merge for wider buckets. After Apache IoTDB's time-window M4.

title: REST catalog
summary: `timelake-catalog`, an Iceberg REST catalog that is optional and can scale to zero, so Snowflake, Trino, Athena and Spark attach to Timelake tables in place. Beyond the standard API it queues commits, caches metadata and plans scans with Timelake's indexes. Planned; the object-store catalog ([spec 3](0003-object-store-catalog.md)) is what is built.

title: DuckDB extension
summary: A loadable DuckDB extension that makes DuckDB Timelake-aware: dedup on read, index-aware scans, the hot tier, and the function library, with the same kernels as the Timelake reader. Plain DuckDB already reads every table ([spec 1](0001-iceberg-tables.md)); the extension closes the gap to the Timelake reader for people who keep DuckDB.

title: Snowflake connection
summary: Snowflake queries Timelake tables in place as Iceberg tables, through the REST catalog or registered metadata files, set up by one command, with time-series helpers mapped onto Snowflake built-ins.

title: Multitenancy
summary: Documented patterns for many tenants: a shared table with a tenant column, a namespace per tenant, or a bucket per tenant, with their isolation and cost, plus credential vending and per-tenant retention, rollups and quotas.

title: Ingestion and rules
summary: A library-first pipeline for ingestion with in-stream rules (thresholds, flatlines, heartbeats, anomalies), deployable embedded, on Lambda, as a container or at the edge, writing alarms to an events table and real-time sinks.

title: Data to events
summary: Typed events produced from data (rules, SQL definitions, pass-through) and published at least once to any event system, in-stream or triggered by commits, with the events table as the durable record.

title: Static read models
summary: Dashboards' usual requests answered by one GET: read models declared with the frontend's Zod schemas, stored as time tiles in the bucket, and regenerated from each commit's snapshot diff.

title: Computed metrics
summary: User-defined Python functions whose results Timelake keeps up to date the way it keeps rollups: recomputing the windows each commit affects.

title: Agent access with permission sets
summary: An MCP server and client operations that let LLM agents find, understand and read time-series data, within permission sets the reader enforces by rewriting plans, with results that fit a context window and every query audited.

title: Device sync
summary: Devices write to a local table and a sync agent moves committed data to the lake: store and forward, resumable, prioritized, exactly once through idempotent batches, with per-device credentials.

title: Edge gateway
summary: A single binary on site that devices send data, metrics, logs and blobs to, which buffers and forwards to the lake, runs rules locally, and serves recent data from its cache when the uplink is down.

title: Server mode
summary: An experiment: the same engine as one long-lived server on local NVMe, with the bucket as the durable copy and Postgres wire and Flight SQL protocols, measured against TimescaleDB before anything is built.

title: Benchmark harness: timebench
summary: One reproducible suite run against Timelake and every alternative with each system's own tooling: TSBS IoT and DevOps plus lake-specific workloads (streaming ingest, late data, maintenance, cost), local and on object storage, every run kept with its commit, and a weekly regression run.

title: Industrial IoT benchmark
summary: A plant historian workload: thousands of tags at mixed rates, gateways going offline and resending, duplicates, every opponent on one table, checked against a reference for correct answers, and reported with cost per month and growth.

title: Agent benchmark
summary: Does an LLM agent answer questions about time-series data more correctly, with fewer tokens and tool calls, when the data is in Timelake? One agent loop against the same data through different arms, scored on generated tasks with known answers.
